title: WordPress Nonce Verification and CSRF Prevention
description: Every state-mutating request (POST, PUT, DELETE, AJAX, REST mutations, admin form submissions) must be guarded with cryptographic WordPress nonces to prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).
rules: Generate nonces in forms using wp_nonce_field( 'action_name', '_wpnonce' ) or wp_create_nonce( 'action_name' ).
Verify nonces in traditional admin form handlers using check_admin_referer( 'action_name', '_wpnonce' ).
Verify nonces in AJAX handlers using check_ajax_referer( 'action_name', 'nonce_key' ).
Verify nonces in custom REST API mutating endpoints via X-WP-Nonce header or permission_callback wp_verify_nonce().
Never process or persist user inputs before verifying the nonce.
anti_patterns: Processing POST/GET state changes without nonce verification.
Using a static or shared predictable string as a nonce.
Calling wp_verify_nonce() but ignoring its return value (failing open).
Using check_admin_referer() inside AJAX handlers (which causes standard HTTP redirect or die instead of JSON error response).

title: WordPress User Capability and Privilege Escalation Prevention
description: Authentication alone is insufficient; authorization must be verified explicitly via capability checks (current_user_can) before executing sensitive administrative or mutating business operations.
rules: Always call current_user_can( $capability ) before processing administrative settings, data exports, schema migrations, or sensitive entity deletions.
Use specific granular capabilities (e.g. 'manage_options', 'edit_posts') rather than checking broad role names directly.
Check capabilities on every AJAX, REST, and admin-post endpoint independently of the menu registration visibility.
anti_patterns: Relying solely on is_admin() or is_user_logged_in() to protect sensitive backend logic.
Checking roles like $user->roles[0] === 'administrator' directly instead of current_user_can().
Assuming UI hidden elements or menu permissions prevent unauthorized API requests.

title: Input Sanitization and Output Escaping Standards
description: All untrusted user input must be sanitized upon receipt before persistence or processing (Sanitize Early), and all variables rendered into HTML/attributes/JS must be contextually escaped (Escape Late) to completely prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
rules: Sanitize strings with sanitize_text_field(), slugs with sanitize_title() or sanitize_key(), emails with sanitize_email(), integers with absint() or intval().
Always unslash before sanitizing: sanitize_text_field( wp_unslash( $_POST['field'] ) ).
Escape HTML body text with esc_html(), HTML attributes with esc_attr(), URLs with esc_url(), textareas with esc_textarea().
Escape rich HTML with wp_kses_post() or custom wp_kses() allowed tag schemas.
Escape inline JavaScript or JSON data with wp_json_encode() or esc_js().
anti_patterns: Directly echoing raw POST, GET, or database variables into HTML templates.
Using strip_tags() instead of standard WordPress sanitization helpers.
Omitting wp_unslash() on superglobals before sanitizing.

title: SQL Injection Defense via $wpdb->prepare
description: All dynamic variables incorporated into database queries must be safely parameterized through $wpdb->prepare() with explicit type specifiers (%s for string, %d for integer, %f for float).
rules: Never interpolate or concatenate dynamic variables directly into SQL query strings.
Use explicit format specifiers: %d for integers/IDs, %f for prices/floats, %s for strings/dates.
For LIKE queries, construct placeholders with $wpdb->esc_like( $search ) and '%s'.
anti_patterns: Direct string concatenation: "SELECT * FROM {$table} WHERE user_id = " . $_GET['id'].
Using addslashes() or mysql_real_escape_string() instead of $wpdb->prepare().
Passing table names or identifiers as %s parameter placeholders (table names cannot be parameterized; validate identifiers against a whitelist instead).
